questions.stem: A student needs to make barium sulfate (BaSO4), which is insoluble. Which two soluble solutions should she mix together?

options.text: Barium chloride solution and sodium sulfate solution
Barium oxide and dilute sulfuric acid
Barium nitrate solution and sodium chloride solution
Barium metal and sulfuric acid

questions.explanation: To make an insoluble salt by precipitation, mix two soluble solutions that contain the required ions. BaSO4 needs Ba2+ and SO4 2- ions. Barium chloride (soluble) provides Ba2+ and sodium sulfate (soluble) provides SO4 2-. When mixed: BaCl2(aq) + Na2SO4(aq) -> BaSO4(s) + 2NaCl(aq). The BaSO4 precipitates as a white solid.

questions.stem: After mixing lead nitrate solution with potassium iodide solution, a bright yellow precipitate forms. What steps should the student take to obtain pure, dry lead iodide?

options.text: Evaporate the entire mixture to dryness
Filter to collect the precipitate, wash with distilled water, then dry in a warm oven
Leave the mixture to cool and scrape off the yellow crystals
Add more lead nitrate to dissolve the precipitate

questions.explanation: The yellow precipitate (PbI2) is collected by filtration. It must be washed with distilled water to remove any soluble impurities (KNO3 and excess reagents). Then it is dried in a warm oven or left to dry on filter paper. Evaporating the whole mixture would also give you the soluble salt (KNO3) as an impurity.

questions.stem: A student writes the ionic equation for the precipitation of silver chloride: Ag+(aq) + Cl-(aq) -> AgCl(s). What are the spectator ions if she used silver nitrate and sodium chloride?

options.text: Ag+ and Cl-
Na+ and NO3-
Na+ and Cl-
Ag+ and NO3-

questions.explanation: The full equation is: AgNO3(aq) + NaCl(aq) -> AgCl(s) + NaNO3(aq). The spectator ions are those that appear unchanged on both sides of the ionic equation - they do not participate in forming the precipitate. Na+ and NO3- remain dissolved in solution throughout. Ag+ and Cl- are the reacting ions.

questions.stem: Using solubility rules, which of the following salts is INSOLUBLE in water?

options.text: Sodium chloride (NaCl)
Potassium nitrate (KNO3)
Lead chloride (PbCl2)
Calcium nitrate (Ca(NO3)2)

questions.explanation: Most chlorides are soluble, but lead chloride is an exception - it is insoluble. All sodium and potassium salts are soluble. All nitrates are soluble. The key exceptions to learn are: lead chloride, silver chloride, barium sulfate, lead sulfate, and calcium sulfate (slightly soluble). These exceptions are important for predicting precipitation reactions.

questions.stem: Why can insoluble salts NOT be made by reacting an acid with a base?

options.text: Acids are too weak to form insoluble salts
Insoluble salts cannot be dissolved, so there is no way to crystallise them from solution
If the salt is insoluble, it would form on the surface of the base and prevent further reaction
Bases do not react with acids to form salts

questions.explanation: If you tried to make an insoluble salt (like BaSO4) by reacting barium oxide with sulfuric acid, the insoluble BaSO4 would form as a coating on the surface of the barium oxide, preventing the acid from reaching more of the base underneath. This is why precipitation from two soluble solutions is the preferred method for making insoluble salts.
